scene-u01-pnew1-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew1-25.text: What we can compute versus what we want: how far apart?

scene-u01-pnew1-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew1-26.text: To judge a model we want how far $\hat f$ is from the true $f$.

scene-u01-pnew1-69.name: text#69
scene-u01-pnew1-69.text:
It depends on one thing:
did the prediction "collude" with this observation?

scene-u01-pnew1-71.name: text#71
scene-u01-pnew1-71.text: Without collusion (independence), the gap is exactly the noise floor.

scene-u01-pnew2-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew2-25.text: A test point took no part in training: the prediction and its noise are independent

scene-u01-pnew2-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew2-26.text: So $\hat f_0$ depends on the training data only, while $\varepsilon_0$ is a fresh draw of noise.

scene-u01-pnew2-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew2-40.text: the test point is not in the training data

scene-u01-pnew2-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew2-66.text: This is why KP01 demands disjoint sets.

scene-u01-pnew2-68.name: text#68
scene-u01-pnew2-68.text: The prediction $\hat f_0$ and the new noise $\varepsilon_0$ do not influence each other.

scene-u01-pnew3-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew3-25.text: Split the "distance to the observation" in two, then square and take the expectation

scene-u01-pnew3-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew3-30.text: $\mathbb E\big((\hat f_0-y_0)^2\big)=\mathbb E\big((\hat f_0-f_0)^2\big)-2\,\mathbb E\big(\varepsilon_0(\hat f_0-f_0)\big)+\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0^2)$

scene-u01-pnew3-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew3-44.text: Three terms, handled one by one; next, why the cross term is 0.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: The cross term vanishes: thanks to independence and zero-mean noise

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: $\varepsilon_0$ and $\hat f_0-f_0$ are independent, so the expectation splits.

scene-u01-pnew4-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew4-28.text: $\mathbb E\big(\varepsilon_0(\hat f_0-f_0)\big)=\mathbb E(\varepsilon_0)\,\mathbb E(\hat f_0-f_0)=0\cdot\mathbb E(\hat f_0-f_0)=0$

scene-u01-pnew4-54.name: text#54
scene-u01-pnew4-54.text: Visible error = true error + noise floor.

scene-u01-pnew4-56.name: text#56
scene-u01-pnew4-56.text: For an unused test point, the computable error exceeds the true error by exactly $\sigma^2$.

scene-u01-pnew5-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew5-26.text: The noise takes two values with probability one half each, so $\sigma^2=1$; the observation is $y_0=1$ or $3$.

scene-u01-pnew5-60.name: text#60
scene-u01-pnew5-60.text: cross term $-2\,\varepsilon_0(\hat f_0-f_0)=\mp 1$, half each, mean $0$

scene-u01-pnew5-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew5-62.text: Both sides equal $1.25$: the formula holds.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: Summed over the whole test set: computable err ≈ true Err + $n_{te}\sigma^2$

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: Add up the formula over all $n_{te}$ test points.

scene-u01-pnew6-33.name: text#33
scene-u01-pnew6-33.text: computable once we have the test labels $y_i$

scene-u01-pnew6-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew6-38.text: distance to the true output; needs $f_i$, unobservable

scene-u01-pnew6-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew6-45.text: Here $\approx$ means equal in expectation, close on one test set; the more test points, the closer.

scene-u01-pnew6-47.name: text#47
scene-u01-pnew6-47.text: err exceeds the true Err by the noise floor $n_{te}\sigma^2$.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: Rearranged: Err ≈ err − $n_{te}\sigma^2$, a numerical example

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: $n_{te}=50$, $\sigma^2=4$, and err $=300$ on the test set.

scene-u01-pnew7-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew7-32.text: err $=300$ (actually computed on the test set)

scene-u01-pnew7-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew7-38.text: Per point: empirical $300/50=6$, true $100/50=2$; the difference $4$ is exactly $\sigma^2$.

scene-u01-pnew7-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew7-40.text: Reading err directly makes the model look much worse than it is (here 3× worse).

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: Watch the identity hold in a computer simulation

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: The identity rests on independence, so we test it by repeating the experiment.

scene-u01-pnew8-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew8-31.text: ② each run: draw 15 training points

scene-u01-pnew8-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew8-34.text: ③ then draw 20000 fresh test points

scene-u01-pnew8-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew8-38.text: with different training data each time

scene-u01-pnew8-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew8-48.text: Will they agree? The next page shows the 300 results.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: All 300 points lie almost exactly on the line $y=x$

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: x-axis $\mathrm{mean}(\hat f-f)^2+\sigma^2$, y-axis $\mathrm{mean}(\hat f-y)^2$ on the fresh test points.

scene-u01-pnew9-337.name: text#337
scene-u01-pnew9-337.text: the largest gap in any single run is only $0.0077$

scene-u01-pnew9-359.name: text#359
scene-u01-pnew9-359.text: The computable error is "true error + noise floor".

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: A straight line is a biased model, yet the identity still holds

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew10-26.text: The truth is a parabola, so no line can ever be right.

scene-u01-pnew10-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew10-46.text: The identity asks for independent test points, not a correct model.

scene-u01-pnew10-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew10-48.text: However biased the model, the identity holds as long as the test points are unused.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: Why the model with the smallest err is the one with the smallest Err

scene-u01-pnew11-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew11-26.text: $n_{te}\sigma^2$ depends on the data only, not on the model.

scene-u01-pnew11-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew11-41.text: The same $200$ is subtracted from both: the ranking is unchanged, $260<300$ and $60<100$.

scene-u01-pnew11-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew11-42.text: (model B's numbers are an added example)

scene-u01-pnew11-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew11-64.text: On an independent test set, the smallest err picks the smallest Err.

scene-u01-pnew12-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew12-25.text: When the premise fails: a used test point makes err too small

scene-u01-pnew12-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew12-26.text: The conclusion has one premise: the test points were truly unused.

scene-u01-pnew12-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew12-28.text:
Test data entered training or chose hyper-parameters
(KP01's two kinds of cheating)

scene-u01-pnew12-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew12-32.text:
$\hat f_0$ colludes with the noise of $y_0$:
$\mathbb E\big(\varepsilon_0(\hat f_0-f_0)\big)\neq 0$, the cross term stays

scene-u01-pnew12-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew12-36.text:
err comes out too small
the model looks better than it is

scene-u01-pnew12-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew12-37.text: By how much are trained-on points under-estimated? The next section shows it with four points.

scene-u01-pnew12-39.name: text#39
scene-u01-pnew12-39.text: The test set must truly be unused, else the model looks better than it is.

scene-u01-pnew13-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew13-25.text: A four-point example: truth, noise, observations

scene-u01-pnew13-59.name: text#59
scene-u01-pnew13-59.text: noise pushes truth to the observation

scene-u01-pnew13-86.name: text#86
scene-u01-pnew13-86.text: Training sees the noisy observations $y$ (orange), not the truth $f$ (blue).

scene-u01-pnew14-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew14-25.text: Two models trained on these four points: memoriser vs straight line

scene-u01-pnew14-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew14-26.text: The memoriser predicts $\hat f_i=y_i$; the line is the least-squares line $\hat f=1.5+0.8x$.

scene-u01-pnew14-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew14-52.text: memoriser: every training point exactly right

scene-u01-pnew14-56.name: text#56
scene-u01-pnew14-56.text: The red line hits every orange point; the green line balances between them.

scene-u01-pnew14-58.name: text#58
scene-u01-pnew14-58.text: The same four points, two very different models.

scene-u01-pnew15-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew15-25.text: Three errors: training error is always lower than the error on new data

scene-u01-pnew15-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew15-41.text: The memoriser learned the noise too: training error $0$, yet worst on new data.

scene-u01-pnew15-43.name: text#43
scene-u01-pnew15-43.text: Both training errors are below the error on new data.

scene-u01-pnew16-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew16-25.text: So training error can neither rank models nor estimate the true error

scene-u01-pnew16-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew16-28.text: ① Both training errors are below the new-data error: they saw these $y$, noise included.

scene-u01-pnew16-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew16-30.text: ② The memoriser has training error $0$ yet is worst on new data.

scene-u01-pnew16-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew16-32.text: ③ The tighter the fit to the training points, the further the training error falls below the new-data error.

scene-u01-pnew16-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew16-34.text: Compare with data that did not train the model: KP01's validation and test sets.

scene-u01-pnew16-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew16-36.text: Next: what happens when a model is too complex? KP05 looks at overfitting.

steps.label: KP04 · 1/16
steps.speakerNotes: To judge a model we want the distance from f̂ to the true f, but f is unseen.

steps.label: KP04 · 1/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: To judge a model we want the distance from f̂ to the true f, but f is unseen.

steps.label: KP04 · 1/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: What we can compute is the distance to the noisy y. How far apart are they?

steps.label: KP04 · 1/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: It depends on whether the prediction colluded with this observation.

steps.label: KP04 · 2/16
steps.speakerNotes: Training data produce the model, which predicts f̂₀ for the test point.

steps.label: KP04 · 2/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Training data produce the model, which predicts f̂₀ for the test point.

steps.label: KP04 · 2/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The test point took no part in training; its noise ε₀ is a fresh draw.

steps.label: KP04 · 2/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So f̂₀ and ε₀ are independent, which is why KP01 demands disjoint sets.

steps.label: KP04 · 3/16
steps.speakerNotes: Substitute y₀ = f₀ + ε₀: f̂₀ − y₀ = (f̂₀ − f₀) − ε₀.

steps.label: KP04 · 3/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Substitute y₀ = f₀ + ε₀: f̂₀ − y₀ = (f̂₀ − f₀) − ε₀.

steps.label: KP04 · 3/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Square and take the expectation: three terms.

steps.label: KP04 · 3/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: First: distance to the truth; third: KP03's σ²; middle: the cross term.

steps.label: KP04 · 4/16
steps.speakerNotes: ε₀ and f̂₀ − f₀ are independent so the expectation splits into E(ε₀)·E(f̂₀ − f₀), and E(ε₀) = 0.

steps.label: KP04 · 4/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: ε₀ and f̂₀ − f₀ are independent so the expectation splits into E(ε₀)·E(f̂₀ − f₀), and E(ε₀) = 0.

steps.label: KP04 · 4/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: What remains: E((f̂₀ − y₀)²) = E((f̂₀ − f₀)²) + σ².

steps.label: KP04 · 4/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The computable error is the true error plus the noise floor σ².

steps.label: KP04 · 5/16
steps.speakerNotes: f₀ = 2, prediction 2.5, noise ±1 half each, so σ² = 1 and the observation is 1 or 3.

steps.label: KP04 · 5/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: f₀ = 2, prediction 2.5, noise ±1 half each, so σ² = 1 and the observation is 1 or 3.

steps.label: KP04 · 5/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Squared errors: (2.5 − 1)² = 2.25 and (2.5 − 3)² = 0.25, mean 1.25.

steps.label: KP04 · 5/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Right side: (2.5 − 2)² + 1 = 1.25, equal. The cross term is ∓1, half each, mean 0.

steps.label: KP04 · 6/16
steps.speakerNotes: The one-point result adds up over the whole test set of n_te points.

steps.label: KP04 · 6/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The one-point result adds up over the whole test set of n_te points.

steps.label: KP04 · 6/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: err is the computable empirical error; Err is the true error and needs f; n_te·σ² is one σ² per test point.

steps.label: KP04 · 6/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: ≈ means equal in expectation, close on one test set. In this chapter err and Err are sums, not averages.

steps.label: KP04 · 7/16
steps.speakerNotes: Rearranging: Err ≈ err − n_te·σ², i.e. 300 − 50 × 4 = 100.

steps.label: KP04 · 7/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Rearranging: Err ≈ err − n_te·σ², i.e. 300 − 50 × 4 = 100.

steps.label: KP04 · 7/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The whole 300 is the err computed on the test set; blue 100 is the true error, red 200 the noise floor that no model can shed.

steps.label: KP04 · 7/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Per point: empirical 6, true 2, the gap 4 is exactly σ². Reading err directly makes the model look much worse than it is.

steps.label: KP04 · 8/16
steps.speakerNotes: True function f(x) = 1 + 2x − 1.5x², noise standard deviation 0.3.

steps.label: KP04 · 8/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: True function f(x) = 1 + 2x − 1.5x², noise standard deviation 0.3.

steps.label: KP04 · 8/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Each run: 15 training points, a fitted line, then 20000 fresh test points.

steps.label: KP04 · 8/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Compute mean(f̂ − y)² and mean(f̂ − f)² + σ²; repeat 300 times.

steps.label: KP04 · 9/16
steps.speakerNotes: Each point is one repetition: x is mean(f̂ − f)² + σ² (needs f), y is the computable mean(f̂ − y)². (Fixed-seed redraw; numbers match the lecture.)

steps.label: KP04 · 9/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each point is one repetition: x is mean(f̂ − f)² + σ² (needs f), y is the computable mean(f̂ − y)². (Fixed-seed redraw; numbers match the lecture.)

steps.label: KP04 · 9/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The gold dashed line is y = x: points on it mean the two quantities are equal.

steps.label: KP04 · 9/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Mean of the 300 runs 0.3501 = 0.2601 + 0.09; the largest single-run gap is only 0.0077.

steps.label: KP04 · 10/16
steps.speakerNotes: The truth is a parabola, so a line is a biased model.

steps.label: KP04 · 10/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The truth is a parabola, so a line is a biased model.

steps.label: KP04 · 10/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: On 400000 fresh points the cross term averages −0.00003 ≈ 0, and the noise's mean square is 0.0900 = σ².

steps.label: KP04 · 10/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The identity asks for independent test points, not a correct model.

steps.label: KP04 · 11/16
steps.speakerNotes: Model A: err 300, minus the floor 200, Err 100.

steps.label: KP04 · 11/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Model A: err 300, minus the floor 200, Err 100.

steps.label: KP04 · 11/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Model B (an added example): err 260, Err 60.

steps.label: KP04 · 11/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: n_te·σ² depends on the data only and is subtracted from both, so the ranking is unchanged: on an independent test set the smallest err is the smallest Err. This is why test error works as a generalisation measure.

steps.label: KP04 · 12/16
steps.speakerNotes: Premise: the test points are truly unused. If test data entered training or chose hyper-parameters (KP01's two cheats)…

steps.label: KP04 · 12/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Premise: the test points are truly unused. If test data entered training or chose hyper-parameters (KP01's two cheats)…

steps.label: KP04 · 12/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: f̂₀ colludes with the noise of y₀: E(ε₀(f̂₀ − f₀)) is no longer 0 and the cross term stays.

steps.label: KP04 · 12/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: err comes out too small and the model looks better than it is. How much for trained-on points? The next section shows it with four points.
